extracted.intended_audience: students of American government and politics; general readers seeking an overview of congressional powers
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter survey of the constitutional powers, limits, and practical operation of the U.S. Congress, with interpretive approaches and illustrative historical examples. Useful for learning what Congress may lawfully do and how debates about constitutionality shape legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation to enumerated powers and necessary and proper
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is limited to the exercise of the powers enumerated in the Constitution and the use of means necessary and proper to carry them into execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts the limited, written powers of Congress with the near-omnipotence of the British Parliament; this restriction profoundly influences debates because measures outside the enumerated powers will be declared unconstitutional and thus not worth discussing. Constitutional doubt generates searching legal inquiry and often dominates legislative debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approaches to constitutional questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Three broad views members of Congress may take when deciding constitutionality: (1) strict construction — narrow reading of powers; (2) liberal (broad) construction — generous reading using the Necessary and Proper clause; (3) pragmatic/legislative approach — legislate and let the Court decide and, if necessary, propose constitutional amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jefferson's strict-construction argument against a federal bank; liberal construction leading to national bank, highways, reclamation projects; Bourke Cockran's quoted view advocating legislation first and judicial resolution later. These approaches shape whether Congress adopts expansive federal measures or refrains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue and expenditures powers (taxing and appropriations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises and appropriate money to pay debts and provide for defense and general welfare, but the power is not unlimited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraints and specifics: indirect taxes/duties/excises must be uniform nationwide; direct taxes (except income taxes from all sources) must be apportioned among states by population; Congress cannot tax exports; cannot tax certain state instrumentalities (per Supreme Court interpretation) such as state salaries or municipal bonds; appropriations for the army may not be made for more than two years; otherwise spending discretion is broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: National defence powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has virtually unlimited powers with respect to national defense: raise and support armies, create and maintain a navy, provide for organization/use of the militia, declare war, and make rules concerning captures and reprisals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits noted: the President is commander-in-chief and military appropriations are limited to two-year periods. Historical and theoretical concerns (e.g., risk of despotism) are discussed; contrast drawn with other systems (e.g., German legislature) to illustrate breadth of Congress's defence authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and business regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may regulate commerce with foreign countries, among the several states, and with Indian tribes; make uniform bankruptcy laws; fix standards of weights and measures; protect authors and inventors; and establish post offices and post-roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commerce is defined broadly (includes transport of commodities, passenger transport, telegraph messages, and carrying oil through pipelines). Determining when a state law is an unconstitutional regulation of interstate commerce can be difficult. Federal bankruptcy law (act of 1898) covers the field and takes precedence over conflicting state laws, though the power is not absolutely exclusive. Bureau of Standards and other administrative details are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents and trademarks (administration and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is entrusted with protection of inventors and registration of trade-marks; it has created a patent bureau (in Interior) headed by a commissioner who issues patents, records applications, and administers appeals and reissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical details: applications are referred to technical examiners, applicants often use attorneys but are not required to, rejected applications may be appealed to the commissioner and courts, patents (as of the period discussed) run for seventeen years, and reissues/extension practices are described; statistics on applications and grants illustrate scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright law administration and reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress establishes copyright law (coverage expanded to books, art, maps, music, etc.) and may extend protection to foreign authors on a reciprocal basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration is by the registrar of copyrights under the Librarian of Congress; historically Congress limited protection to U.S. citizens until the 1891 act allowed reciprocal protection; historical copyright term discussed (twenty-eight years with possible twenty-eight-year renewal under earlier law; new law noted 1909). The copyrights division does not make infringement examinations analogous to the patent office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post offices and post-roads (exclusive federal power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishment of post offices and post-roads is a power exclusively conferred on Congress, covering mail transportation within and among states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionally linked to commerce power; federal control over the whole domain of mail transport is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign relations and immigration powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress's direct power over foreign relations is limited (President and Senate lead treaty-making), but Congress may regulate foreign commerce including immigration, create consular/diplomatic posts and pay emoluments, define and punish piracy and offenses on high seas, and establish uniform rules for naturalization (generally viewed as exclusively federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress can influence foreign-related matters via commerce and immigration regulation; states may in practice grant political rights to aliens (e.g., voting), despite federal naturalization power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary system regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress exclusively regulates the monetary system: coin money, regulate its value and the value of foreign coin; states are forbidden to coin money or emit bills of credit and may only make U.S. gold and silver coin legal tender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Constitution doesn't expressly authorize paper money, Congress has exercised that power and the Supreme Court has sustained it. States are explicitly constrained from independent currency actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to define crimes and provide punishments (criminal jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress's power to define crimes and punishments is narrowly limited: treason is narrowly defined in the Constitution; Congress may punish counterfeiting, crimes on the high seas, offenses against laws of nations, and define crimes against federal laws, but the general domain of criminal law is left to the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the states control most criminal law, actions may be crimes in some states and innocent in others. Congress may create federal offenses where necessary to give effect to federal authority (e.g., theft connected with transportation of mail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special sessions and timing of Congress; lame-duck effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may call special sessions of Congress to convene on extraordinary occasions; regular scheduling (sessions beginning months after elections) can produce lame-duck legislatures that pass measures opposed by the recent popular vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: special call July 4, 1861 (Civil War), April 1913 (tariff). The delay between election and seating of representatives allows an outgoing House to pass important measures contrary to recent electoral preferences; critics argue defeated members legislate poorly or are susceptible to corruption/inducements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No constitutional provision for instructing members by constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution provides no mechanism for constituents to 'instruct' their members of Congress; state legislatures sometimes pass instructions but cannot compel resignation or enforce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although unenforceable, instructions occur in practice; representatives are nevertheless very sensitive to party leaders and local political pressures. There is no penalty for violating state instructions, illustrating the constitutional independence of federal legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate characteristics and influence (organization and informal power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate is smaller and generally composed of older, more experienced men with longer terms; it often contains political experts and exerts disproportionate influence through appointments, treaty ratification, party leadership, and unlimited debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: Senators can overshadow the House on technical legislation; Senate control over appointments and treaties increases its political weight; party and state organization, plus senatorial leadership, can pressure House members. Criticisms include ties to corporate interests ('millionaire's club') and conservatism due to economic connections; examples given include the Republican convention of 1900 where Senators dominated key roles.
